The Carnival Plays On

Word comes from [carnival_town.GetName]: brightly painted wagons have drawn up outside the town walls in time for the fair. There are tumblers and a fire-eater, a fat strongman in a sack hood, jesters with bells on their caps, and a tiny band of pipers no taller than a child. They are led by a tall man in a smiling mask, who calls himself only the Master. The Burgomeister writes to you in raptures. The fair has never drawn such crowds, the coin is flowing, and the troupe promises a play for the feast day in honour of [Root.GetTitledFirstName] - if [Root.GetSheHe] will only come and watch.

Word comes from [carnival_town.GetName]: a commedia troupe has set up its stage in the piazza, a gaudy wagon hung with masks of every kind. There are acrobats and a fire-eater, a fat strongman in a sack hood, a Pantalone with a nose like a gourd and a band of tiny pipers. Their leader is a tall man in a smiling mask who calls himself only the Master. Rumour says a rival prince has paid them to make fun of you, and the merchants are delighted - they say nothing has drawn such crowds in years. The Master promises a performance in your honour for the feast day.

Word comes from [carnival_town.GetName]: a fiesta troupe has arrived for the saint's day, with painted giants on poles, big-headed dancers, bells, drums and a straw effigy to burn when the feast ends. Its leader is a tall man in a smiling mask who calls himself only the Master. With him come a fat strongman in a sack hood and a band of tiny pipers who are already the darlings of the town's children. The priests grumble, but the people love them. The Master promises a play for the feast in honour of [Root.GetTitledFirstName].

Word comes from [carnival_town.GetName]: a band of mummers has come to the peasants' fair. Your knights laugh at them as a show fit only for peasants. There are tumblers and a fire-eater, a fat strongman in a sack hood, jesters with bells on their caps and a band of tiny pipers, and they are led by a tall man in a smiling mask who calls himself only the Master. The peasants have not been so merry in years. The Master begs leave to perform before his lord on the feast day, so that the noble [Root.GetTitledFirstName] may laugh with his people.

Word comes from [carnival_town.GetName]: wandering players have come to the market with a bear on a chain, a tall painted wagon, jesters with bells, a fat strongman in a sack hood and a band of tiny pipers. Their leader is a tall man in a smiling mask who calls himself only the Master. The young folk crowd round them, but the babushkas spit three times and make the sign against evil whenever the wagon goes by. They say no honest player travels so far into Kislev with the snows so close. The Master promises a play for the feast day in honour of [Root.GetTitledFirstName].
Let them play! The people deserve some joy.
Let them stay - and have them watched.
Someone you trust will keep an eye on the troupe. A witch hunter, wizard or other seer at court is best, otherwise your spymaster.
We want no strangers here. Send them on their way.
The Carnival takes the road out of your lands.
Arrest the lot. Painted vagabonds are trouble.
The guard will seize the troupe and throw them in the cells.

The guard took the players in the night, all but the Master and his wagon, which were nowhere to be found. Now the gaoler reports that every one of the prisoners is dead. They swelled in their cells like drowned dogs and burst, and the stink is unbearable. Two of the guards have taken to their beds with fever. At dawn a farmer saw a painted wagon going down the road out of your lands, with no horse to pull it, and he says it was singing.
Burn the bodies, and the cells with them.

Since the troupe came to [carnival_town.GetName], the milk sours in the pail, and the butter will not come however long the dairymaids work the churn. The dogs howl all night at the wagons and will not go near them by day. The town's cats have vanished. People are laughing it off, but the old women are not laughing.
Look into it.
Sour milk is no matter for the court.
It is Strigany witchcraft. Drive them out!

A child of [carnival_town.GetName] woke screaming in the night. She had dreamt of a fat old grandfather who laughed and laughed and held her on his knee, and she kept saying the same words over and over: "Flies, flies, eat up his eyes!" By the next night a dozen children had the same dream. In the day they sit with the tiny pipers from the Carnival and learn their songs.
Look into it.
Children have bad dreams. Let it be.

[carnival_watcher.GetTitledFirstName] saw [carnival_jester.GetFirstName], the Carnival's favourite jester, take a girl's hand in the square, bowing and joking until she laughed. By the morning a sore had opened on her palm, weeping a yellow-green ooze that smells sweet, like overripe fruit. Her mother has wrapped it and says it is nothing. Two others who laughed with [carnival_jester.GetFirstName] have the same sore.
Look into it.
Send a physician and pay for her care.

At dusk the tiny pipers struck up a tune, and half of [carnival_town.GetName] followed them out of the gate in a long line, dancing and laughing, three times round the town walls. Nobody can say afterwards why they went. Some came home with mud to the knees, singing a song none of them knew. Some did not come home at all, and their families say they must have gone to the next village.
Look into it.
A dance at the fair. What is the harm?
Your watcher will look into it. A witch hunter, wizard, Ice Witch, Grail Knight or Damsel of the Lady, or a sharp spymaster, stands the best chance of seeing through the paint.
The troupe stays, and grows bolder.

[carnival_watcher.GetTitledFirstName] comes to you pale and shaking. [carnival_watcher.GetSheHe] went close to the Master's wagon after dark and looked through a crack in the boards. There is a pentagram chalked on the floor, glistening as if it were wet, and something sat on it that was not a man. The players' masks are not masks. Under the paint are sores, and under the sores... The tiny pipers are not children, but things with too many teeth. This is no troupe. It is the Carnival of Chaos, the plague-show of the Lord of Decay that the witch hunters whisper about, and it means to play for [carnival_town.GetName] at the feast.

[carnival_watcher.GetTitledFirstName] has watched the troupe for days and found nothing - only painted players, a bad smell from the wagons, and a Master who bows too low and smiles behind his mask. Whatever is happening in [carnival_town.GetName], nobody can say that the Carnival is to blame.
Gather the guard. We strike before the show.
Keep watching them.
You know what the Carnival is. You can strike before the play.

The play is called The Emperor's True Face. On a ramshackle stage that is also the wagon's dressing room, a fat player in a paper crown waddles about, belching and breaking wind, while the crowd roars. A mock Knight Panther rides a hobby-horse in circles, crying "A horse, a horse, the Emperor is a horse!" Then the Emperor turns, and he wears your face. The jesters move through the crowd, slapping backs and squeezing hands. From the seat of honour, [Root.GetTitledFirstName] can see the Master at the back of the stage, very still, watching you rather than the play.

The piece is Orfeo and Pustulate, a mock opera. A fat tenor with a nose like a rotten gourd sings his way down into the underworld to bring back his beloved, who rises from her bier covered in boils and kisses him full on the mouth. The piazza screams with laughter. Between the verses the Pantalone mimics you so well that even your courtiers laugh. The jesters move through the crowd, slapping backs and squeezing hands. Behind the stage the Master stands very still, watching you rather than the play.

The piece is A Midsummer Nightmare. The lovers wander into a wood, where a fat fairy king in a crown of mushrooms marries them all to each other and then to a donkey, while the painted giants dance and the drums pound. The town roars. The donkey wears a mask very like your face. The jesters move through the crowd, slapping backs and squeezing hands. Behind the stage the Master stands very still, watching you rather than the play.

The piece is Papa Noigul's Festering Children: a fat, kindly grandfather who loves all his children and gives each a gift, a sniffle for one, a boil for another, a cough for a third. The peasants laugh until they weep. Then a mummer comes on in tin armour on a hobby-horse, crowned and pompous, and Papa Noigul gives him the best gift of all. Your knights are not laughing, but the peasants are. The jesters move through the crowd, slapping backs and squeezing hands. Behind the stage the Master stands very still, watching you rather than the play.

The players give a puppet tale, Papa Noigul's Festering Children: a fat grandfather in a fur hat who comes out of the snow to give every child in the village a present, a sniffle for one, a boil for another, a cough for a third. The market laughs and stamps in the cold. Then a puppet boyar comes on in a great fur coat, and Papa Noigul gives him the best present of all. The babushkas have gone home. The jesters move through the crowd, slapping backs and squeezing hands. Behind the stage the Master stands very still, watching you rather than the play.
Ha! Let them mock me. It is only a play.
I have seen enough of this filth.
Something is wrong with those players...
Look closely at the players. You may see what they are, or get too close to a jester.
Watch the Master, not the stage.
The Master will notice you watching.
The jesters squeeze the hands of you and your court. Some of you may fall sick.
You see the sores beneath the paint. When the sun sets, you will be ready.

Between the acts the Master comes to your seat and bows very low. Up close the mask is not quite a mask, and he smells of rot and honey. "My lord honours us," he says. "Grandfather loves all his children, even the proud ones. He sees how you are burdened - the coughs in winter, the aches, the long fear of the grave. He would take all that away. Take his gift, and my players will spare this little town and play instead for whomever you please. Refuse him, and we will play for you at sunset." Somewhere behind the stage, a great many flies begin to buzz.

Between the acts the Master comes to your seat and bows very low. Under the mask his face is a ruin, and he smells of rot and honey. "Brother," he whispers. "I knew Grandfather's own when I saw them. This town is yours, so we will not play for it. But we take a great deal of feeding, and Grandfather is generous to those who feed us. Take his gift, and tell us where to go next."
I accept Grandfather's gift.
Get away from me, you stinking thing.
Guards! Seize him, now!
Try to take the Master before sunset. A strong arm, a sharp mind and a seer at court help. If you fail, you are wounded and the show goes on.
The Master may leave behind a Plague Cart: a band of daemons and diseased cultists that will follow you.
The Master bows. "The town is spared, my lord. We leave tonight. Now tell us: where would you like us to play?"
Go and play for my rival.
Go and play for my enemy.
Wherever the road takes you.

The guard is ready before dawn, torches and steel, and the wagons stand dark at the edge of [carnival_town.GetName]. Inside, something is singing in a voice like a drain. If you strike now, you may end it before the show begins.
Burn the wagons with them inside.
Storm the camp!
Send for the witch hunters. This is their work.
The witch hunters take over the hunt. The Carnival is destroyed, but the glory is theirs.
The Ice Witch will freeze them where they stand.
Your Ice Witch calls the cold of the north down on the Carnival. Rot does not work in the frost. The Master is taken, frozen to the wagon seat.
A Grail Knight will challenge the Master.
A Grail Knight of your court rides out to challenge the Master to single combat in the Lady's name.
Pay Tilean blades to do the work.
You fight the Carnival in the square. Being forewarned, having good martial skill, paid blades or a seer at court all help.

At sunset the play ends, and the paint begins to run. Under it is not skin. The costumes split, and out of them come the Plaguebearers, one-eyed and horned, droning their endless count of Grandfather's plagues. Nurglings spill from the Plague Cart like maggots from a wound, and the jesters - the Tainted - laugh as they tear at the crowd. [carnival_brute.GetFirstName] the Brute tears off his sack hood, and half his face slides off with it. The Master has thrown back his mask. His face crawls with flies, and he is laughing too. All around you, the people of [carnival_town.GetName] are screaming.

At sunset the paint begins to run, but you are ready. Your guard is already in the square, steel drawn and torches lit, when the costumes split and the Plaguebearers come out of them, one-eyed and horned, droning their endless count of Grandfather's plagues. Nurglings spill from the Plague Cart like maggots from a wound. [carnival_brute.GetFirstName] the Brute tears off his sack hood, and half his face slides off with it. The Master throws back his mask and his face crawls with flies. "Ah," he says. "An audience that knows the ending. How tiresome."
Hold the square! Cut them down!
Fire the wagons! Burn it all!
Get me out of here, and bar the town gates behind us!
Wait! Master, let us talk...

The square is held. [carnival_brute.GetFirstName] the Brute lies dead across the stage with a dozen wounds that do not bleed, the Brethren lie dead among the stalls, the Tainted are burning, and the daemons have fled back into the Cart, droning in fury. But when the smoke clears, the Master and the last of his wagons are gone. Wheel ruts lead out of the town, with no hoof marks between them.
After him!

The square is lost. By the morning [carnival_town.GetName] is a town of the dead and dying, its well fouled, its people bloated in their doorways, and its dogs dead in the street. Those who lived are not much better off. The Master went through the town before he left and took a finger from every woman and child who still lived, crying "You're my wife now!", and many of them walked away after his wagons and did not look back. Your stewards are still counting who of your own household is gone.

The gates of [carnival_town.GetName] were barred behind you, with the town and its people inside. All night the guards on the walls heard the screaming, the laughter and the droning count. By morning it was quiet. When the gates were opened, the town was a town of the dead, bloated in their doorways. The few who lived were each missing a finger, and they say that the Master led the rest away singing. Your stewards are still counting who of your own household is gone.
Burn the dead. Count the living.
The town is ravaged by plague for years. The pestilence may spread.

The Master of the Carnival kneels in chains in the yard, his mask gone and his face a weeping wound full of flies. He is laughing softly. "Burn me if you like," he says. "Grandfather loves me. I will be in his garden before the smoke clears, and the Carnival will find another Master. There is always another Master."

The Master of the Carnival is dead in the dust, still laughing as the last of the flies left his mouth. The Plague Cart has stopped singing. Without him, the daemons he called have faded back to wherever they came from, and the Brethren run like frightened children. His mask lies beside him in the mud, still smiling.
Burn him, and the Cart with him.
Give him to the witch hunters. They will know what to do.

The Master is gone, with the Plague Cart and a few of his wagons. His trail is easy to follow: dead crows, soured wells, and children who sing a song they never learned. If you follow it, you may catch him before he reaches another town. If not, he will be someone else's trouble.
Hunt him down.
You ride after the Master. The chase may take some weeks.
Let him go. Let him rot somewhere else.

The trail leads to a village two days down the road. It is empty. The doors stand open, the bread is still on the tables, and the cows are bloated in the byre. There is not a living soul there. The wagon ruts lead on.

At a crossroads you find the place where the Carnival made camp. There is a ring of burned grass, a broken mask, and in the middle a neat pile of fingers - dozens of them, small ones mostly. The ruts lead on, and they are fresher now.

A little girl sits alone by the road, singing to herself. When she sees your riders she smiles and holds up her hand, which is missing a finger. "The Master says to hurry," she says. "He says you are nearly too late." The ruts are fresh. The Cart cannot be far.
Ride on! We have him now.
Enough. We turn back.
The trail goes on.
The Master slips away across the border.

You find the Plague Cart in a dead orchard at dusk, with the Master standing on its tailboard chalking a pentagram on the boards. The chalk lines glisten, and through them you can smell a garden - a warm, sweet, rotten garden full of flies. "Too late, too late!" he sings. "Grandfather's door is opening, my lord!" A few of his Brethren are between you and him, and they have knives.
Face him myself!
You fight the Master hand to hand. He is a sorcerer of Nurgle, and the fight could cost you your life.
Guards! Take him alive!
The Great Unclean One

The Master's chanting rises to a shriek, and the Plague Cart splits open like a rotten fruit. Something heaves itself out of it - and out, and out, far bigger than the wagon that held it. A mountain of green-grey flesh, its belly torn open on a nest of chattering Nurglings, its single horn crusted with filth, its face beaming with a vast, gentle, grandfatherly joy. A Great Unclean One stands in [carnival_town.GetName], and it is delighted to meet you all. Where its shadow falls, the people sicken where they stand. One of your household is already dead at its feet, and the stench alone is driving men mad. "Such lovely children," it rumbles. "Come, come. Grandfather has gifts for everyone."
Run! Run and do not look back!
Stand and fight! For the living!
Face a greater daemon of Nurgle. Few mortals survive it. A wizard or seer at your side gives you a slim hope.
Kneel before Grandfather's chosen.
the Great Unclean One
the Brute

Word comes that the painted wagons of the Carnival have been seen far from your lands, on the road to a fair in the lands of [carnival_host.GetTitledFirstName]. They say the Master is already promising a play for the feast day.
Let it be their trouble.

In a dream you see a fair in the lands of [carnival_host.GetTitledFirstName], with painted wagons, laughing children and tiny pipers. The Master turns from the stage and bows to you, very low, and the flies rise in a cloud from under his mask. Grandfather's children are playing for your enemies.
Play well, my children.
Carnival in Town
A troupe of travelling players has come for the fair, and the people are merry.
Visited by the Carnival
The Carnival of Chaos played here. The town is half empty, and the plague lingers in its wells and houses.
Burned Wagons
The Carnival's wagons were burned at the edge of town, and the fire took more than the wagons.
Sealed Town
The gates were barred on the living while the Carnival played inside.
Grandfather's Favour
This character took the gift of the Carnival Master. Coughs and fevers pass them by, but the faithful sense something rotten about them.
Ended the Dance of Death
This character ended the Carnival of Chaos, and the people sing about it.
Mocked by the Players
This character walked out of a play that mocked them. The people are still repeating its best lines.
the Carnival Master
The Carnival Master's Mask

The smiling mask the Master of the Carnival of Chaos wore over what was left of his face. It is always slightly warm and slightly damp, and on quiet nights it whispers. A follower of Nurgle hears it gladly. Anyone else should burn it, but nobody ever does.
Veterans of the hunt may swear themselves to your banner: a band of plague-hunters at half upkeep.
